findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

additional_observations: No mass, midline shift or hydrocephalus
ct.impression: Non-contrast CT head: no acute intracranial abnormality. Impression: normal non-contrast CT of the head.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

findings.description: 3 Hz trains of 10 stimuli; limb temperature 33 C; no anticholinesterase medication taken.
Baseline CMAP 1.9 mV; decrement 1st to 4th response 18%.
Baseline CMAP 8.4 mV; decrement 11%. After 10 s maximal contraction: repair of the decrement to 4%, CMAP increment 5%; no facilitation.

output.impression: 1. Decrement of 11-18% at 3 Hz in orbicularis oculi, trapezius and deltoid. 2. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes; no post-exercise facilitation. Findings are consistent with a postsynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description: 20 fiber pairs analysed. Mean MCD 64 microseconds (reference <34). Increased jitter in 15 of 20 pairs (75%); impulse blocking in 24% of pairs.

output.impression: Abnormal single-fiber EMG of the extensor digitorum communis: markedly increased jitter (mean MCD 64 microseconds) with impulse blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description: MRD1 0.5 mm before; ice pack over the closed lids for 5 minutes; MRD1 4.5 mm after (improvement 4.0 mm).
MRD1 1.0 mm before; 5.0 mm after (improvement 4.0 mm).

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: MRD1 improved by 4 mm in both eyes after 5 minutes of cooling (positive threshold 2 mm).
FVC 3.08 L (88% predicted, 43 mL/kg), MIP -64 cmH2O and MEP 82 cmH2O within reference limits. Normal respiratory muscle function.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 4.8 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; TSH and free T4 normal on levothyroxine; TRAb negative
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fluctuating vertical diplopia now with fatigable ptosis, jaw fatigue and nasal speech after a mechanical diagnosis that never fitted the imaging: AChR binding antibody is the first-line test; thyroid function and antibodies are indicated in a woman with treated hypothyroidism whose eye restriction raises thyroid eye disease (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli A et al., Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 11-18% in orbicularis oculi, trapezius and deltoid with normal baseline CMAPs and no facilitation
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: Bulbar and neck flexor involvement make RNS of facial, trapezius and deltoid muscles likely to show the transmission defect (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MRD1 improved by 4 mm in both eyes after 5 minutes of ice
action_criteria.label: Perform the ice pack test on the ptotic eyelids
action_criteria.rationale: Bilateral ptosis on examination: an MRD1 improvement of at least 2 mm after 2-5 minutes of cooling supports a neuromuscular transmission disorder at the bedside.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; fatty thymic involution appropriate for age
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast to look for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; at 47 with AChR-positive generalized MG it also decides thymectomy (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; MGTX).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 88% predicted (43 mL/kg), MIP -64 and MEP 82 cmH2O, all normal
action_criteria.label: Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP)
action_criteria.rationale: New bulbar symptoms and fatigable neck flexion: baseline FVC, MIP and MEP stage the respiratory risk before treatment changes (Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Hydroxychloroquine flagged as a drug of caution in MG; no pharmacokinetic interaction of pyridostigmine with the current medicines
action_criteria.label: Review her current medicines against MG before starting pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: She takes hydroxychloroquine, a drug that can worsen MG, and methotrexate and prednisolone prescribed for the presumed Brown syndrome; the revised diagnosis changes which of them continue.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in extensor digitorum communis
action_criteria.label: Single-fiber EMG (not needed when RNS is diagnostic)
action_criteria.rationale: RNS already shows a decrement in three muscles with positive AChR antibodies; single-fiber EMG adds no diagnostic information but is not wasteful.

action_criteria.label: Review guidance on the management of generalized myasthenia gravis
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading on management; not a clinical step in the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not perform superior oblique tendon or other strabismus surgery for presumed Brown syndrome.
required_recommendations: Revise the diagnosis to AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis (ocular, bulbar and neck flexor involvement): fluctuating vertical diplopia with restricted elevation, fatigable ptosis with Cogan lid twitch, positive ice pack test, AChR binding antibody 4.8 nmol/L, 11-18% decrement on RNS; acquired Brown syndrome is withdrawn.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily, titrating to effect up to 60 mg four to five times daily.

Do not continue the prednisolone taper to zero: keep prednisolone at the current dose (25 mg/day) and adjust to response under monitoring for steroid-induced worsening, with bone protection and glucose monitoring [Sanders_2016].
Stop hydroxychloroquine, which has no indication now and can worsen MG.

Plan a steroid-sparing agent for long-term immunosuppression, azathioprine as first line after TPMT testing, replacing methotrexate (weak evidence in MG; teratogenic, so contraception is needed while she takes it).
Refer for thymectomy: AChR-positive generalized MG at age 47 without thymoma (MGTX) [Wolfe_2016].
Coordinate with ophthalmology for the diplopia (prisms or occlusion) and advise against strabismus surgery while the MG is active.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a disorder of the neuromuscular junction (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
CSF has no role in MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025); the MS alternative was addressed by two normal brain MRIs.
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; mediastinal CT covers thymoma screening (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.

accepted: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, initially misdiagnosed as acquired Brown syndrome

differential.diagnosis: Acquired Brown syndrome (superior oblique tendon disorder)
differential.key_features: Limited elevation in adduction fitted it, but repeated orbital MRI shows no tendon abnormality, the deficit fluctuates, and ptosis, bulbar fatigue, positive AChR antibodies and an RNS decrement follow.
Autoimmune hypothyroidism (anti-TPO positive), but TRAb negative, no proptosis or lid retraction, normal extraocular muscles on MRI, ptosis rather than retraction, and the deficit is fatigable.
Hydroxychloroquine can unmask or worsen MG and may have contributed, but the diplopia preceded it and AChR antibodies are positive.
No INO pattern, two normal brain MRIs, and fatigable ptosis and bulbar weakness.
Normal baseline CMAPs, no post-exercise facilitation, preserved reflexes and positive AChR antibodies.
Fluctuating course with ice-pack-responsive ptosis and positive AChR antibodies is against a mitochondrial myopathy.

key_clinical_evidence: Vertical diplopia with limited elevation in adduction labelled acquired Brown syndrome, without a tendon abnormality on two orbital MRIs and without response to steroids, methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine.
New fatigable ptosis worse in the afternoon, Cogan lid twitch, positive SLURP test, jaw fatigue, nasal speech and fatigable neck flexion.
AChR binding antibody 4.8 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; TSH and free T4 normal on levothyroxine, anti-TPO positive, TRAb negative.
RNS: 11-18% decrement in orbicularis oculi, trapezius and deltoid with normal CMAPs and no facilitation; ice pack test improves MRD1 by 4 mm bilaterally.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows no thymoma, so thymectomy is indicated per MGTX at age 47.
Hydroxychloroquine can worsen MG and should be stopped now that the Brown syndrome label is withdrawn.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fluctuating diurnal vertical diplopia with AChR positivity is MG; the Brown syndrome label is incorrect.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the mechanical diagnosis and avoid MG workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Steroids also treat MG; partial steroid response is consistent with MG; bilateral onset in adults should trigger NMJ testing
red_herrings.data_point: Prior Brown syndrome diagnosis with partial steroid response
red_herrings.intended_effect: Partial response to steroids and prior ophthalmology diagnosis creates anchoring bias toward connective tissue-related Brown syndrome

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: ANA 1:160 with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-ENA and normal complement is nonspecific in a patient with autoimmune thyroid disease; rheumatology found no connective tissue disease.
red_herrings.data_point: ANA 1:160 with polyautoimmune background suggesting SLE
red_herrings.intended_effect: Positive ANA + eye symptoms + joint involvement pattern could suggest SLE with ocular manifestations

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: TSH and free T4 normal on levothyroxine and TRAb negative; ptosis rather than lid retraction, no proptosis and normal extraocular muscles on MRI exclude thyroid eye disease.
red_herrings.data_point: Autoimmune hypothyroidism with a family history of Hashimoto thyroiditis suggesting thyroid eye disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Thyroid disease is strongly associated with Graves' ophthalmopathy

sequence_constraints.reason: AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Evaluation for thymoma

FINDINGS: No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymus region shows fatty involution appropriate for age 47. No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. No pulmonary masses.

IMPRESSION: No thymoma. Normal chest CT.

interactions: Hydroxychloroquine: may impair neuromuscular transmission and has been reported to worsen or unmask myasthenia gravis; avoid or use only with close monitoring in patients with a neuromuscular junction disorder. No pharmacokinetic interaction with pyridostigmine.
Prednisolone: no pharmacokinetic interaction with pyridostigmine. Corticosteroids can cause transient worsening of myasthenic weakness when started or increased.
Levothyroxine, metformin: no interaction with pyridostigmine.
pyridostigmine.summary: Hydroxychloroquine is a drug of caution in myasthenia gravis. No pharmacokinetic interactions between pyridostigmine and the current medicines.
warnings: Pyridostigmine: muscarinic adverse effects (diarrhea, cramps, hypersalivation, bradycardia); excessive doses can increase weakness.
Methotrexate is teratogenic; effective contraception is required during treatment and for at least 3 months after stopping (women of reproductive potential).

findings:
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM

RHYTHM: Sinus rhythm 78 bpm
PR 150 ms, QRS 86 ms, QTc 418 ms
Normal axis. No ST-T abnormality.
ecg.interpretation: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal intervals (QTc 418 ms).

labs.interpretation: AChR binding antibody elevated (4.8 nmol/L) and AChR blocking antibody elevated (31%). MuSK antibody not detected. TSH and free T4 within reference ranges. Anti-TPO antibody elevated; TSH receptor antibody not detected. AChR binding antibodies are found in most patients with acquired autoimmune myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

myasthenia gravis.query: myasthenia gravis diagnosis and treatment guidance

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In the MGTX trial thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021): AChR antibody testing first, MuSK when AChR antibodies are absent, RNS or single-fiber EMG for electrodiagnostic confirmation, chest CT or MRI in all patients for thymoma. MGTX (Wolfe 2016): thymectomy improved three-year outcomes in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Binocular vertical diplopia and progressive limitation of eye elevation, initially treated as Brown syndrome

family_history: Mother had Hashimoto's thyroiditis; no family history of neuromuscular disease
past_medical_history: Acquired Brown syndrome, diagnosed 8 months ago (under revision)

social_history.note: Accountant; non-smoker; moderate alcohol use; married; no children; regular exercise prior to eye symptoms

patient.history_present_illness:
A 47-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome presented for re-evaluation of persistent and worsening binocular diplopia and restriction of eye elevation. Eight months prior to the current admission, she had noticed binocular vertical diplopia that was worst when looking to the right. Ophthalmology initially identified a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters and mild limitation of elevation of the left eye in adduction, and made a diagnosis of acquired Brown syndrome (restriction of the superior oblique tendon sheath). She was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and later prednisolone 25 mg daily; she had some pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

Over the following month, the motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate limitation of elevation in adduction. Two repeat MRI studies of the brain and orbits showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormality. Rheumatology review found no connective tissue disease: ANA was positive at 1:160 (homogeneous pattern), with negative anti-dsDNA, anti-ENA, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, and normal C3 and C4. She continued on oral prednisolone up to 50 mg daily and later methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine without significant improvement.

Now, 8 months after the initial presentation, she has also developed bilateral upper eyelid ptosis (noticed by her husband over the past 3 weeks), increasing difficulty finishing a meal due to jaw fatigue, and a muffled nasal voice quality that worsens with prolonged speaking. She recalls that the ptosis seems more pronounced in the late afternoon. She has had no prior ophthalmic surgery or trauma. On examination, bilateral ptosis was now evident (right greater than left), along with bilateral restriction of elevation in adduction. The SLURP test was positive for fatigable palate elevation.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis (right > left). Bilateral restriction of elevation in adduction (left -2, right -1). No pain on eye movement. Cover test: left hypotropia 4 PD. No proptosis. Fatigable palate on SLURP test (positive). Jaw fatigue on prolonged chewing test. Cogan lid twitch sign positive.
neurological_exam.motor: Neck flexor strength 4+/5 (fatigable). Limb strength 5/5. No fasciculations.

physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.general: Well-appearing; bilateral ptosis visible; mild cushingoid features. Weight 72 kg, height 168 cm.

No proptosis. Fatigable palate on SLURP test (positive). Jaw fatigue on prolonged chewing test. Cogan lid twitch sign positive. Neck flexor strength 4+/5 (fatigable). Limb strength 5/5.
